opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Alex, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Glad to. I'll try to separate what I'd say at a rally from what I'd say at home, since that's what you're after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say even a modest tool is owned by a handful of giant firms, and that's a power problem whether it changes jobs or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, not much. I use it to draft grant reports, which frees up time. I'd still be worried about who controls the data and the platforms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running our worker rights programme. Push for transparency rules on workplace monitoring. Use the time saved on grant reports to do more outreach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my usual way. That's my baseline.

S0.say: Even a modest tool is owned by a handful of giant firms, and that's a power problem.
S0.think: Little changes for him personally, but who controls the data and platforms still worries him.
S0.do: Runs the worker rights programme, pushes for monitoring transparency rules, and uses saved time for outreach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fewer entry-level jobs is a choice companies are making, not a law of nature. Workers should have a say in how this rolls out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow change is the best chance we get to build rules before it's too late. That actually gives me some hope. My own job is safe-ish. Funders still want humans running campaigns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build a coalition with unions on AI in the workplace. Write model contract language for bargaining. Train our members on their rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but with something to work on.

S1.say: Fewer entry-level jobs is a choice companies make, not a law of nature. Workers should have a say.
S1.think: Slow change is a chance to build rules in time, which gives him hope; funders still want humans running campaigns.
S1.do: Builds a coalition with unions, drafts model contract language on AI, and trains members on their rights.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but with work to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a transfer of power from workers to shareholders, plain and simple. Nobody voted for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the fight I've trained for. But I also have no savings, and my funding comes from foundations that panic in downturns. And honestly, a lot of what I do is writing and reporting, which these agents do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job is writing and reporting. Would your organisation replace you with an agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not me, probably, I do the people side too. But the junior staff, the comms person, I could see our board asking. And I'd be the one who has to say no, and maybe lose that fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run hard on a campaign for notice periods and severance when firms automate. Diversify our funding so we're not hostage to one donor. Quietly update my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and wired. Scared and fired up at once.

S2.say: This is a transfer of power from workers to shareholders. Nobody voted for it.
S2.think: It's the fight he trained for, but he has no savings, foundation funding is fragile, and AI agents do much of his writing work well.
S2.do: Campaigns for notice and severance rules on automation, diversifies funding, and quietly updates his CV.
S2.feel: Anxious and wired, scared and fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest grab of wealth in history and we have to take it back. Public stakes in AI firms, a wealth tax, a dividend for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange truth: this is the moment movements are built for. People would finally listen. But the foundations that pay me are funded by the same stock market that's booming. I'd be arguing against my own funders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Organise every laid-off office worker I can reach. Push for a people's dividend. Look for funding from unions and small donors instead of big foundations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and more alive than I've felt in years.

S3.say: This is the biggest wealth grab in history. Public stakes in AI firms, a wealth tax, a dividend for everyone.
S3.think: It's the moment movements are built for, but his funders' money comes from the same booming market he'd be fighting.
S3.do: Organises laid-off office workers, pushes a people's dividend, and seeks union and small-donor funding.
S3.feel: Alarmed, yet more alive than in years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say once they've automated the care homes and the building sites, the question is who owns the machines. If it's a few billionaires, that's not a market, it's a kingdom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now the working-class base I organise is hit too, not just office people. That's a much bigger movement, but also a much more desperate one. Desperate people don't always turn left. That frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build alliances with care workers', builders' and farm workers' groups straight away. Push for public ownership of robots in care. Make sure our people aren't pulled toward blaming migrants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Hopeful about the movement, scared of where anger goes.

S4.say: Once they've automated care homes and building sites, the question is who owns the machines. A few billionaires isn't a market, it's a kingdom.
S4.think: Hitting manual workers too makes a bigger but more desperate movement, and desperate people don't always turn left.
S4.do: Builds alliances with care, building and farm worker groups, pushes public ownership of care robots, and counters blame toward migrants.
S4.feel: Alarmed, hopeful about the movement but scared of the anger.
